                               UNITED STATES OF AMERICA

                       FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

    PJM Interconnection L.L.C. Study                   )

    Ohio’s State Agreement Approach Request;           )

                         COMMENTS FOR CONSUMER PROTECTION
                                          BY
                        OFFICE OF THE OHIO CONSUMERS’ COUNSEL


I.        INTRODUCTION

          The Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel (“OCC”), on behalf of Ohio’s 4.5 million

residential utility households, respectfully submits these comments regarding PJM

Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) Submission of a Study Agreement in Furtherance of the State

of Ohio’s State Agreement Approach Request. The Study Agreement concerns the construction

of a massive 10 GW artificial intelligence (“AI”) data center, generation and transmission

development at the former Portsmouth Gaseous Diffusion Plant in Pike County, Ohio known as

the “Flagship Project.”1

          OCC welcomes the potential for economic development, infrastructure modernization,

and other benefits the Flagship Project may bring to Southern Ohio. Ohio’s economic

development goals and the protection of residential utility consumers should go hand in hand.

Agreements supporting major energy projects must ensure that the financial risks and

infrastructure costs associated with those projects are borne by the entities that benefit – not

shifted to Ohio families and other utility consumers.



1
    PJM Study Agreement Request, FERC Docket No. ER27-126-000 (Oct. 13, 2026), at 2.
            To protect Ohioans from potential financial and reliability risks, the establishment of

enforceable consumer protections and transparency as the study progresses is paramount. FERC

must ensure that the proposed Study Agreement does not expose Ohio residential consumers to

additional costs or reliability risks associated with this extraordinary new electric demand. FERC

should recognize that the State of Ohio’s sponsorship of the study does not constitute an

agreement by Ohio residential consumers to finance the project or assume the developer’s

financial risks. There must be no presumption that Ohio residential consumers are responsible for

any of the Flagship-related transmission facilities, network upgrades, or associated costs.

           SB Energy, a data center developer backed by big-tech behemoths SoftBank, OpenAI,

and Nvidia,2 has committed to pay $4.2 billion in transmission investment costs associated with

the project.3 An additional $33 billion for the planned 9.2 GW gas-fired generation facilities will

be paid for through the U.S.-Japan Strategic Trade and Investment Agreement.4 But the specific

cost allocation and recovery mechanisms have not yet been approved.

           These upfront financial commitments are encouraging. However, a developer’s promise

to protect ratepayers is not the same as legally enforceable protections. More is needed to protect

non-data center consumers from paying for other project costs and ensuring the Flagship Project

delivers the promised benefits. The developer’s obligation to pay should cover all incremental

transmission facilities, network upgrades, financing costs, and potential stranded investment.

           Infrastructure facilities are long-lived assets with costs that will extend far beyond the

financial pledges highlighted in headlines and press releases. Enforceable safeguards should be

 in place before construction commitments to make sure these costs are properly allocated to the

data centers causing the costs. Ohioans also should not pay costs related to unforeseen

construction delays, cost overruns, or stranded investments in the event Flagship Project is

downsized or is not fully deployed.

          FERC should also ensure that existing consumers are also protected from indirect costs.

The project could also affect capacity prices, transmission rates, energy prices, and reliability

throughout Ohio and the PJM region. Payment for directly assigned transmission infrastructure

alone does not eliminate those broader consumer impacts.

          The Ohio Federal Energy Advocate (“FEA”) requested that PJM implement the SAA set

forth in PJM’s Operating Agreement to help shield Ohioans from Flagship Project costs and to

promote State of Ohio policies to provide consumers with “adequate, reliable, safe, efficient,

non-discriminatory and reasonably priced retail electric service.”5 OCC appreciates the FEA’s

action and also supports Ohio’s policies regarding electric utility service. However, as the FEA

acknowledges, “[t]he details of the SAA and specific cost-allocation and recovery approach will

be subject to regulatory proceedings before the [Public Utilities Commission of Ohio

(“PUCO”)], which will issue its findings through an order in the PUCO case.”6 Before allocating

costs to retail consumers, upfront consumer protections for transparency, regulatory oversight,

cost allocations, and independent review should be built into the SAA.

II.       THE FLAGSHIP PROJECT AND THE STATE AGREEMENT APPROACH

          The Flagship Project is a partnership between multibillion dollar technology and

investment conglomerate SoftBank and Ohio Power Company (f/k/a AEP Ohio) to “redevelop



5
    R.C. 4928.02(A).
6
    PJM Study Agreement Request, at Schedule A (Ohio State Agreement Approach Request).


                                                       3
 [U.S. Department of Energy] land, modernize energy infrastructure, and develop advanced

computing in Southern Ohio.”7 PJM explains that the Flagship Project

                     is an integrated artificial intelligence (“AI”) data center,
                     generation, and transmission development centered at and around
                     the former United States Department of Energy (“DOE”)
                     Portsmouth Gaseous Diffusion Plant in Pike County, Ohio. It has
                     an initial 800MW phase served under Ohio Power Company’s
                     (“Ohio Power”) Data Center Tariff, and the expansion being
                     evaluated under the Study Agreement comprises approximately
                     9,570 MW of additional load and 10,170 MW of gross new
                     generation, supported by three proposed 765 kV transmission lines
                     and related infrastructure.8

            The transmission infrastructure necessary to accommodate the Flagship Project is

currently estimated to cost $4.2 billion.9 SB Energy has committed to pay these costs. SB Energy

has also committed to fund the costs incurred by PJM in conducting SAA studies, which could

exceed $1 million.10 An additional $33 billion will be spent to construct 9.2 GW of gas-fired

generation to serve the Flagship Project.11 This will be funded through the U.S.-Japan Strategic

Trade and Investment Agreement.

            Earlier this year, the Ohio FEA requested that PJM initiate the SAA process under PJM’s

Operating Agreement “to ensure the costs associated with the transmission lines and associated

infrastructure constructed by AEP Ohio or its designee are assigned to Ohio to then be further

allocated to SB Energy, which has committed to pay the costs.”12 However, the SAA is just the

 beginning of the process to evaluate the proposed data center loads and whether the proposed

transmission and generation will be sufficient to the serve the needs of the Flagship Project and

maintain service reliability for other consumers in Ohio.13 If they are not, PJM may identify

additional transmission investment needs. According to PJM, the “Study Agreement further

provides that the studies will yield planning-level estimates of needed transmission facilities and

does not itself select transmission projects or designated entities, establish cost allocations, grant

specific transmission rights, or address rate recovery in any manner.”14

            Before the Flagship Project is included in PJM’s Regional Transmission Expansion Plan

(“RTEP”), PJM will work with parties to the Study Agreement to determine a cost allocation

methodology to be filed with FERC to assign costs to Ohio, which will then be recovered

through wholesale formula rates.15 Further details of the SAA, including retail cost allocation

and recovery, will be considered through subsequent proceedings before the PUCO.16

III.        CONSUMER PROTECTION RECOMMENDATIONS

            OCC appreciates the Ohio FEA’s request for PJM to invoke the SAA process to facilitate

the Flagship Project and allocate costs of the project to SB Energy in accordance with its

commitment to pay for $4.2 billion in planned transmission and infrastructure investment. OCC

recognizes that the Flagship Project could potentially provide significant economic benefits to

Southern Ohio and modernize transmission infrastructure that could serve state policies

promoting safe and reliable service at reasonable rates. At the same time, protections should be

included in the SAA process to make sure non-data center consumers in Ohio do not bear the



13
     PJM Study Agreement Request, at 9.
14
     Id. at 10.
15
     Id. at 17.
16
     Id.


                                                   5
 financial consequences in the event the Flagship Project fails to deliver the benefits for Ohioans

as promised.

       OCC urges the Commission to ensure that the proposed Study Agreement for the

Flagship Project does not expose Ohio residential consumers to additional costs or reliability

risks associated with this extraordinary new load. The State Agreement Approach raises

important questions about consumer financial responsibility, regulatory oversight, and the

appropriate allocation of costs.

       A.      The SAA and subsequent cost allocation and recovery proceedings should
               establish safeguards to protect non-data center customers from paying for
               the Flagship Project’s incremental costs and any costs due to construction
               delays, overruns, downsizing and unused capacity.

       SB Energy has committed to pay $4.2 billion toward the plans for transmission and

infrastructure necessary to accommodate the Flagship Project. However, PJM may determine

through the Study Agreement that more infrastructure is required to reliably serve the project.

Separately, there will be additional operating and maintenance costs, as well as costs for

upgrades, financing, and other project-specific costs. There could also be costs from construction

delays or cost overruns. There could be costs if the project is downsized or not fully completed.

There could be indirect costs of the project including its impact on capacity prices, transmission

rates, energy prices, and reliability throughout Ohio and the PJM region. The question is who

pays for such costs? SB Energy (or the companies that fund it) should pay. SB Energy’s data

center complex will be the cost-causer of 9,750 MW of additional load and the primary

beneficiary of Flagship Project.

       Safeguards should be put in place to protect non-data center customers from these

additional costs. Ohio Power’s existing data center tariff, which will apply to Flagship Project’s

first 800 MW, already contains important provisions that protect consumers from costs caused by


                                                 6
 data centers such as requirements for financial collateral, minimum demand charges, and exit

fees. Yet it is unclear what, if any, similar consumer protections would apply for the 9,750 MW

of additional load Flagship Project will bring.

       The Commission’s recent initiatives addressing large-load interconnections recognize the

importance of preventing costs caused by new large loads from being shifted to existing

consumers. Those same principles should inform the Commission’s review of the Flagship Study

Agreement. The Commission should also ensure that the Flagship arrangement does not

circumvent or undermine applicable consumer protections adopted through its ongoing

proceedings addressing large-load interconnections.

       All these issues should be considered as part of the Study Agreement to determine cost

allocation, recovery, and other issues regarding the Flagship Project. Similarly, any

determinations regarding cost allocation and recovery should consider SB Energy’s executed

service agreements (along with its agreements with data center tenants), financing agreements,

construction permits, and energization schedules. Such safeguards will help protect non-data

center consumers from paying costs for overruns and construction delays.

       Parties to the SAA assert that the new transmission infrastructure to service the Flagship

Project will benefit non-data center consumers and lower electric utility rates in the future. That

is great news for Ohioans struggling to pay what seem to be never ending rate increases for

essential utility services. But the Flagship Project benefits – at present – are speculative and

unquantified. Before any costs of the Flagship Project are allocated to non-data center customers

based on purported project benefits, transparent cost/benefit studies should be conducted to

determine the correct amount of costs to allocate to non-data center consumers. Any cost studies

should consider historical usage patterns, projected future demand for all customer classes, and



                                                  7
 the specific benefits each class receives from the Flagship Project infrastructure. OCC has long

called on the PUCO to more fairly allocate transmission charges passed through to residential

utility consumers retail rates.17

        B.       The Study Agreement and subsequent proceedings to implement the
                 Flagship Project should be transparent, preserve meaningful regulatory
                 oversight and open to consumer participation.

        The rapid growth in AI load interconnection and investment in transmission

infrastructure has resulted in significant increases in charges to Ohio consumers. This

underscores the need for more transparency in PJM’s transmission planning processes. The

Study Agreement and subsequent inclusion of the Flagship Project in PJM’s RTEP process must

be grounded by demonstrated need, prudent engineering, transparent planning assumptions,

project cost-effectiveness and a planning record sufficient to permit meaningful consumer review

and independent audits. These safeguards should be established before significant investments

are undertaken.

        This Commission’s recent actions reflect an increasing emphasis on transparent planning

processes, meaningful stakeholder participation, cost-effective analyses, and well-supported

planning records. In Order No. 1920, the Commission concluded that more forward-looking and

transparent transmission planning is necessary to ensure that transmission investments remain

just and reasonable over the long term. While that rule principally addresses long-term regional

transmission planning, the policy objectives it advances – including transparency, robust

planning assumptions, and meaningful stakeholder engagement – are equally relevant here as

PJM undertakes its study of the Flagship Project through the SAA.




17
 See e.g. In the Matter of the Application of Ohio Power Company to Update Its Basic Transmission Cost Rider,
PUCO Case No. 26-47-EL-RDR, OCC Comments for Consumer Protection (Feb. 24, 2026).


                                                       8
         The need for transparency with respect to the Flagship Project is amplified by existing

shortcomings with PJM’s Attachment M-3 planning process for local transmission projects and

supplemental transmission projects. OCC has described the lack of transparency in PJM’s local

and supplemental transmission planning processes and the adverse impact on retail consumers

through its filings in Ohio in FERC Docket EL23-105-000.18 The same needs for transparency

and consumer participation OCC describes in that proceeding will be required to protect Ohioans

as PJM moves forward with the Flagship Project study and in subsequent regulatory proceedings

to determine appropriate cost allocations and recovery.

        To the extent any transmission owners in PJM propose Supplemental Projects that are

caused by or otherwise related to the Flagship Project, FERC should require transparency

regarding those proposals as part of its approval of this Study Agreement. Identification of

needed transmission upgrades identified by PJM as required for regional reliability is insufficient

to ensure that all needed transmission upgrades associated with the Flagship Project are

transparent to consumers. Supplemental Projects, which escape PJM’s review except for a do-no-

harm analysis, that are related to the Flagship Project must be transparent to the PUCO and to

consumers to make sure that the project sponsors are paying the full costs of the project. The fact

that the PUCO and the Ohio Power Siting Board do not review many or any of these

Supplemental Projects, which ultimately are transmission facilities subject to this Commission’s

jurisdiction, the Study results must include an identification of the proposed Supplemental

Project facilities and costs needed to provide service to the Flagship Project.




18
  See e.g. Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al., FERC Docket EL23-105-
000, Complaint (Sept. 28, 2023); OCC Motion to Lodge (April 11, 2025); OCC Motion to Expedite Action and
Motion to Lodge (Aug. 27, 2026).


                                                       9
        Project presentations made to PJM through the Study Agreement should include

additional information regarding the basis for projected load growth. Without disclosing

confidential commercial information, Ohio Power should identify the extent to which projected

SB Energy’s anticipated demand is supported by executed service agreements with data center

tenants, meaningful development milestones, or other objective indicators demonstrating the

likelihood that the projected load will materialize. If it does not, non-data center consumers in

Ohio could be on the hook for paying infrastructure investment costs that would not otherwise

occur but for the Flagship Project.

       Finally, transparency in PJM meetings and other regulatory proceedings regarding the

Flagship Project is also encouraged for consumer protection. PJM’s decisions regarding the

Flagship Project could have enormous consequences for non-data center consumers in Ohio.

Public (nonconfidential) versions of cost/benefit studies, allocation methodologies, construction

development plans, agreements, and other studies should be made available for public review.

Decisions regarding the Flagship Project should not be developed through closed-door

discussions or processes that leave Ohio’s non-data center consumers and their representatives

unable to understand who advocated for particular outcomes and why. Open meetings, accessible

materials, meaningful opportunity for public and consumer participation, and a clear record of

the basis for PJM’s decisions regarding the Flagship Project would promote accountability and

public confidence.

IV.    CONCLUSION

       The Flagship Project has tremendous potential to bring substantial benefits to Ohioans

and to promote the state’s policies supporting the provision of safe, reliable, and reasonably

priced electric utility service. But extreme care must be taken to ensure the promised benefits

materialize without imposing costs on non-data center consumers in Ohio. Many residential

                                                 10
 electric utility consumers in Ohio simply cannot afford to pay the additional costs. All financial

risks related to the Flagship Project must reside with the big tech companies who are driving the

costs. Accordingly, OCC respectfully requests that the Commission require PJM to implement

OCC’s recommendations.
